To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the phase behavior of charged liposomes can be regulated by the addition of counterions to the solution, that the phase behavior depends strongly on pH, and that the phase behavior is determined by the membrane charge density and the membrane charge density of the counterions.
(i) lipid phase behavior is governed by the lipid ion content, (ii) the ion content is regulated by ion binding to the lipid, and (iii) the ion binding is regulated by pH.
the phase behavior and fusion of charged lipids depend on the ion loading of the membrane.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of solvent ions as a key regulator of membrane fusion.
the regulation of the physical properties of charged membranes and their fusion by the binding of counterions.
the role of ions in lipid membrane phase behavior and fusion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lipid phase behavior is regulated by ion binding and that the ion switch regulates the membrane phase behavior.
the membrane curvature is not a function of only lipid composition, but rather a result of the interplay between the lipid and the ion composition.
the membrane phase state is a result of a balance between lipid-lipid interactions, lipid-ion interactions, and ion-ion interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
lipid membranes are not only a two-component system but rather a three-component system that is regulated by the solvent.
the ion switch regulates the membrane phase behavior by controlling the ion binding to charged lipids.
lipid membranes are not only regulated by their intrinsic lipid composition and their curvature, as previously thought, but also by their ion content and the surrounding ion concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ion content of membranes, and not the lipid headgroup charge, determines the physical state of charged lipid assemblies, which has important implications for membrane biology and technology.
lipid phase behavior is a direct result of lipid-solvent interactions, which can be tuned by the lipid charge, ion concentration, and ion binding affinity.
the ion loading of membranes is a key regulator of membrane fusion, and that the lipid phase theory must be expanded to include solvent ions to fully understand the behavior of charged membranes.
